own_scenes.family: Nueva York: Def Jam, Queens y la edad de oro
own_scenes.desc: El periodista de Billboard Robert «Rocky» Ford, que intuyó el futuro del género, quiso con J. B. Moore un single navideño que volviera cada año; buscando artista dio con un joven promotor de fiestas de Queens, Russell Simmons, que le presentó a Kurtis Blow, b-boy convertido en MC que pinchaba en el Night Fever Disco de Hollis. «Christmas Rappin’» (1979), con Larry Smith al bajo y Denzil Miller a los teclados, entre James Brown y Chic, se pinchó hasta la primavera; Kurtis Blow fue el primer rapero fichado por una multinacional (Mercury) y «The Breaks» (1980) el primer disco de oro del hip hop. Simmons, que creía en los artistas como marcas en una época de discos de 12 pulgadas desechables, puso su foto en la portada. Kool Moe Dee: con Kurtis Blow aprendimos qué era un estribillo.

refs.q: Putting Kurtis Blow’s picture on a 12-inch cover was probably the best thing that I ever did from a branding perspective.
refs.para: I believed in the artists as artists. Putting Kurtis Blow’s picture on a 12-inch cover was probably the best thing that I ever did from a branding perspective. It was so unheard of. And I did it with the help of Robert Ford and J. B. Moore, of course. We’d wait, build up the excitement, the anticipation, and here comes the album.
refs.chapter: Cap. 3: What in the World Is This?

refs.q: Kurtis Blow was the first one to bring the hook into the equation
refs.para: Kurtis Blow was the first one to bring the hook into the equation, and that’s when I truly understood this was going to be more prominent than I thought it would be. Because hip-hop was not an industry yet. It’s just something we’re doing in the street. It’s not a real art form yet. It’s just what we are doing because we love it and we’re passionate and we’re kids and we’re making names doing it.
